And at the end, Mr. Lasic makes it incumbent upon the commanders to implement this order by the 22nd of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to ask my colleague to check the number of the document. Either that's not the right document or this isn't in point 9 of that document, because we don't have what she read out. So check the number, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. You're quite right. It should have been point 11, which comes after point 10 in the document. Thank you for drawing my attention to that. So it's point 11 or para 11. And there's a gap here, a hole there. Anyway, it's the second paragraph under point 10. Is that all right now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, since we put that right, tell us, please, if Mr. Lasic in this way is, in fact, ordering the assistant commander of the Operation Zone for IPD, his assistant, telling him what he should do in order to implement this order?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, that's right. He's telling him to do his job and to explain to people what has happened and what should be done. And it is the duty of the brigade commander to tell his men to do their job properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Now, Mr. Praljak, when you say it is the duty of the brigade commander to tell his men to do their duty and do their -- perform their jobs, when we were talking about SIS and IPD, you said that it was their duty and obligation to act accordingly and that at the same time it was their duty to do so; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Praljak, does that apply -- does the same apply to the other assistants, assistant commanders; for example, the assistant for mobilisation and so on, is it the same thing? Is it their duty to carry it out in a professional way? Does it apply to the other assistants, except the IPD assistant? To all the others, does it apply?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the military sense, yes. But let me tell you why this was introduced, and I can quote you one or two examples, why this method was introduced. Let's assume that the brigade commander appointed his assistant and that the assistant for SIS -- that there's no parallel structure. And if the brother of the commander of a brigade commits a crime, for example, in the classical chain of command in the Western countries, he could tell the assistant for SIS, It's my brother, forget about that problem. Now, here parallelism was introduced precisely because of that, because the assistant for SIS was not appointed by the brigade commander, because there's this parallel structure, and because he has to reject that kind of order.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I don't understand your example at all. And let me tell you why I don't understand what you said. If you are talking about a hypothetical situation, then we must, first of all, establish the facts, and that is that not a single assistant, either SIS or IPD, were appointed by the commander. Everybody below the commander, all the appointments below that, were the obligation of Mr. Stojic, and that is indubitable. And we showed how those appointments were made at the proposal of the brigade commander, in agreement most often -- let me be precise, most frequently along with the agreement of the Main Staff. This would be done by Mr. Stojic. We also demonstrated, using the example of the document by Mr. Siljeg, when it came to the Kupres Battalion, that the dismissal was done in the same way; that is to say, that the commander makes a proposal that so-and-so be dismissed from his duty, but that does not exclude the logics of the following: that the commander must point out if one of the assistants is not performing his job properly, then he must propose that he be replaced and dismissed. And, secondly, if the assistant commander in a brigade issues an order to his -- I beg your pardon. If the brigade commander issues an order to his assistant for SIS which goes against the grain of the rules of service, in hierarchal terms, in the chain of command, should he have addressed the higher level, which is the assistant commander of the operation zone for SIS? Did this hierarchy assist within the HVO from the assistant commander for SIS of the operational zone right down to the battalions? Did that hierarchy exist?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and vis-a-vis the head of the SIS, too, the chief of SIS. So that testifies to this parallel system. He refers to his zone, and this other one refers to the chief of SIS.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Praljak, I can't agree with you there, again, because the SIS Administration or the IPD are not parallel organs, there are no parallel organs, and we heard testimony from both Mr. Bagaric and Vegar and Mr. Bandic, and they explained in very precise terms what their role was. They were professional organs, and they were not any parallel type of organ. And you said, yourself, today that their function was quite different from the command chain, and I'm talking about the chain of command, and I'm going to carry on asking you questions because I wish to demonstrate --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you've made an observation, let me say that they were not professional. Mr. Bandic bore arms and had to arrest people in given situations. So what you were talking about, in professional terms, was not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You mentioned Mr. Bandic and said that he had to make arrests. Now, let me ask you a question, and if you can, answer it; if not, never mind. I wasn't intending to ask you this. When what happened happened in Stupni Do, we saw, from the testimony given by Mr. Bandic, that at that time he, together with Mr. Petkovic, was in Stupni Do and they left together.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour. They were not in Stupni Do.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do apologise. You're quite right. They were in Kiseljak, they were in Kiseljak, right, during the events in Stupni Do.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, to whom did Mr. Petkovic issue an order to carry out investigative procedures? Was it to Mr. Bandic or Mr. Rajic, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to both of them, as far as I remember, because both of them had to submit reports about what had happened up there. But this does not deny the fact of me asking Bandic here whether, if he came across rape, Would you have the right and duty to arrest the culprit, the perpetrator?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, you're not right again. That order was not issued to both men. It was issued exclusively to Mr. Rajic. But Judge Antonetti --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President. I'm going to object to counsel's just arguing with the witness, which is really what this has sort of evolved into in the last couple of minutes. He says one thing, counsel disagrees. It's ultimately for the Trial Chamber to make its decisions, but it's not really appropriate -- it's not proper cross-examination. It's just really an argument, which isn't helpful to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, let me just respond to that, Your Honours. I think I have the right to put my case to the witness, so it was in that framework. But I'll conclude with this discussion, because it's quite obvious that my questions and my case is not confirmed by Mr. Praljak, so I don't want to continue discussing the topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, through the questions that have been put, you have understood that there's an official issue, whether the minister of defence plays a role when it comes to conducting investigations and seizures conducted by the military prosecutor. If a crime is committed somewhere and the SIS conducts an investigation, placed under the control of the SIS -- let me repeat slowly. General Praljak, the questions which Ms. Nozica has just put to you are essential questions because they have to do with the role played by the minister of defence or the head of the Defence Department. In the event a crime is committed, does he have a role to play or does he have no role, because this role is a role that should be the one of the brigade commander, and the brigade commander has the police, the military police, and the SIS to do the job? When a crime is committed, therefore, for the military prosecutor to be seized of the case, the brigade commander needs to conduct an investigation. He can give instructions to the person in charge of the military police or of the SIS to conduct the investigation. A while ago, we saw a document which was a good illustration of this since the document stated, You have until the 17th of September, if I remember correctly, to address to the competent authorities of the military prosecutor the entire report. If the minister of defence has no role to play, then this role should be played by the brigade commander, and the brigade commander reports to the HVO commander, i.e., you, yourself. So this is an essential question. Ms. Nozica has put a series of questions to you, has shown you a whole series of documents, and you're saying, No, the SIS is part of another chain of command. Ms. Nozica said, Well, I do not share your point of view. We shall finish off with this question. What is your final position, Mr. Praljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My final position has been stated several times, and it's quite clear. What does the chief of SIS -- what purpose does he serve and what does the SIS -- what purpose does the SIS serve? The chief of SIS appoints people, regardless of who proposed them. He appoints men, they're his men, and they are duty-bound, on the basis of the laws and rules, to conduct investigative proceedings, regardless of whether the command of a brigade or company issues orders to that effect or not. If a brigade commander or battalion commander or company commander learns about something he will issue an order, but that is not a necessary condition for them do their job properly. The military police, within the frameworks of SIS, is duty-bound to conduct investigations together with them and prepare them for the military prosecutor or investigator. That is their basic duty and task. They are attached to the brigades and battalions, of course, because that's where things happen. And so my answer is crystal clear, because that's how it was. So who files reports, you'll be able to see that, who processes them, who uncovers possible perpetrators. The chief of SIS and the chief of the military police deals with that, and there are two structures. Why would you have a chief of SIS if they're stopped at the brigade or at the operation zone? What purpose would the service perform, then, what purpose would it serve? And professional assistance, such as the FBI, or any other police, or any Secret Service, is there to uncover the perpetrators and to enable those perpetrators to be taken into custody and to allow the investigative judge to have the facts at his disposal and to raise an indictment thereupon. So it's not the duty of a brigade commander. If a brigade commander learns that something has happened, he must secure the site, post some soldiers there to stand guard or tell the military police to do that. That's his duty, for God's sake. There's no dilemma on that score. Now, the fact that they write orders, that these people have to do their job, their work, that's not true and correct, because otherwise you wouldn't need a SIS organisation or a defence department, a military police. They wouldn't be needed. Why have a chief who is not responsible for anything, has no duties, and does nothing? And I wanted to quote examples of why that was put in that way, Your Honours, precisely to show that -- and those services should exercise control over the brigade commanders. The assistants for SIS had the remit of controlling brigade commanders to ensure that they were not engaged in any untoward actions, and then they were to send back that information to the chief of SIS. And then Mr. Stojic was duty-bound to inform me, and so on. So they are parallel systems of control and supervision. It's -- it was set up because of control and supervision. If the assistant for SIS was not doing his job properly, then it was the duty of the commander to inform people about that, but it was the duty of the SIS chief to say that the brigade commander wasn't doing his job properly and that he was interfering, stealing, or whatever. That's how things should have functioned. Of course, there were difficulties within the SIS and within the military police, and with the commanders of the units themselves. Otherwise, we wouldn't have had so many documents written, warning them to prevent, to incarcerate, to investigate, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness Praljak, I have followed everything you have said. I believe I've understood. I would just like to check something out with you. Let's take document P2030, P2030. This document is signed by the Brigadier Lasic. This is an order that contains several items. We have, in paragraph 3, the following: Brigadier Lasic is asking for all of the soldiers and members of the HVO to stop wearing black uniforms. After having given such an order, what happens next? Does this brigadier stand idle and wait for the parallel services to step in or does he remain in control of this order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour Judge Mindua, he can follow the movements, he -- so Brigadier Miljenko Lasic is walking around the front-line, and if he sees a soldier in a black uniform, he will take him to task. But since in the operational zone there are several brigades, of course, it is the duty now of his assistants, including the assistant for SIS, IPD, and the military police to tell him, In such and such platoon there are those people who are in contravention of your order. And not only to tell him that, but pursuant to his order, they must bring those people into custody, recommend a punishment to him that he would then impose, and they must take off their uniforms without the assistants. And if the assistants don't do the job that they have to do, he cannot do his job, in turn. He cannot control four or five brigades which are in his area. So he became aware of the problem, and then he, quite properly, instructs his assistants to do their job. One of them -- one of the tasks is to remove the black uniforms because they were saying that we looked like -- well, the troops got those black uniforms, somebody brought them, and this was associated with some Nazi or fascist uniforms, Mussolini's uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, the example quoted by my colleague is an excellent one, because just look at item 11. Look at what is stated in item 11. Mr. Lasic, who represents the military authority, takes a whole series of decisions. The black uniforms -- the issue about the black uniforms has been mentioned, but other things as well. And here he says that the assistant commander for IPD shall organise meetings in the units to brief the troops about the obligations arising from this order. This person, Mr. Lasic, asks the IPD officers to hold meetings. They then are not going to turn to Mr. Stojic to ask him what they need to do. I assume the order was obeyed. I don't see that there is a parallel chain of command here, when I look at this order.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you can see it, but nobody wants to see it. First of all, they don't have to consult Mr. Stojic. That's not Mr. Stojic's problem. It's the problem of whoever is in charge of the IPD. IPD is aware of the fact who and in what way reached the demarcation. It was all -- yeah, and he is asking from the services that are under his charge to explain to the troops something that has nothing to do with the military, so the meaning of these obligations for the future of the people living in those areas. So an agreement was reached, a military agreement, in those areas. But now how to explain to the people the sense of it in the broader political sense? To do that, one must use the system that is already in place and that is charged with it, and this is the IPD. So, for instance, in the Croatian Army I would organise that, and I would say, This agreement between Franjo Tudjman and whoever has a political significance in this sense, in that sense, because people are not well informed. This is not what the brigade commander must do, but the systems that are attached to him, including the IPD. Of course, it was always an effort to have teachers, educated people, in the IPD who would then be able to convey to people what this is all about. So this is what he wants from them, and they are the ones to do it; not, however, within the framework of what you call or what you say, their subordination. They have at their disposal their meetings and to see what this is all about, and with politicians, and then they can explain to the people how this agreement came about, and why people were supposed to withdraw to the barracks, and why General Pellnas managed to do that, and so on and so forth. But we know what this is all about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I have -- something puzzles me with this document. Perhaps there is a mistake in translation. Would you be so kind and just read the date of the document? On the first page, you have: "Mostar, 22nd," and the next word?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "April."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I find it strange that this is an order dated of 22nd April, and in three different points, number 6, 9 and 12, the commander, Mr. Lasic, orders the order to be completed by 2.00 of the same day. Isn't that a bit strange?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour Judge Trechsel. This agreement was reached with General Pellnas, who was there, and then he witnessed this attempt to calm the situation in Mostar down, and the agreement that Mr. Pellnas managed to achieve with the parties are -- it's implemented with Mico Lasic in accordance with the time schedule. The dead-line for this and that is such and such. The HVO units are to go to Tihomir Misic Barracks and to Heliodrom. The BH Army was supposed to go to the Southern Camp, as far as I can recall. I talked to General Pellnas at that time because he sought a meeting with me, but I didn't want to ask him about this because this was not really -- there wasn't anything of significance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I am not convinced at all by your answer. This is an order. It's not an agreement; it's an order. It's called "Order," and it doesn't say at what time of that day the order is issued, but it requests all sorts of obligations to be met by 2.00 on the same day. And somehow to me this simply doesn't make sense. But maybe you have no answer, and then you say, I have no answer, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have an answer, but you assume that there are some schemes there and now this doesn't fit into those frameworks that you are imagining. It's not necessary to say, in every order, this is in reference to a conversation and so on. This is wartime. People are drafting their documents quickly because they have to implement an agreement by such and such a date. And it's not necessary, just because we are here in court, Well, you should have drafted it in such and such a way so that everybody in this courtroom understands it. It's perfectly reasonable because there was an agreement where Mr. Pellnas spoke about it quite well, and if you remember that, in light of that, this order is quite clear, and it was all about the hours because at the time conflict was already looming, the BH Army was all ready to attack, and later on it, on the 9th of May, it actually occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to add something, but I shall give the floor to my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: What is meant by "removal of all combat shelters," and how many were there? That's number 6.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, on the demarcation line in the Bulevar and so on, this was set by General Pellnas. Well, if you expect that the conflict would break out, there are the places where people were. Shelters were erected by the BH Army on the left-hand side and by the HVO on the right-hand side. And if you remember the agreement, the BH Army was supposed to move out of the Mostar Hotel. They refused to do it. And then Mr. Pellnas went there, and it was an arduous situation. And in the end, well, some of them refused to move out. So a way was sought to calm the situation down in the town, for the troops to go back to the barracks, and for the joint military police to take over control of the town. And you can see here that Brigadier Lasic is also sending this for the information of the Military Police Battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay. That would be vacation -- vacate command post, not remove them. Maybe it's a mistake in the translation. I leave it at that, but I'm not convinced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, while looking at the document in B/C/S, I have realised the following --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Trechsel, I don't want to leave this hanging. What is it that Judge Trechsel is not convinced; the clarity of the agreement that was signed previously and that General Pellnas spoke quite clearly about here? And this is also sent to the 4th Corps of the BH Army. The orders were identical. The identical orders were issued by the BH Army. And again it was sent for the information of the Military Police Administration, so in accordance with the agreement that was reached through the mediation of General Pellnas and the Spanish Battalion of the UNPROFOR to implement everything that is written here. What's unclear about it? To set up a joint military police teams of the HVO and the BH Army that would patrol the town. Well, those patrols were to be dressed in the same uniforms, without any insignia, to avoid a situation where somebody would perhaps fire on them because it's impossible to distinguish Croats from Muslims by their physiognomy. So I really don't understand what's unclear here. If there's anything that's unclear, please ask me. In paragraph 4, it says "a joint team."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I will tell you. It's the time element. In a few hours, this order must go to everyone whom it addresses, and then they must -- again it goes to other commanders who must give orders, and these orders must be executed. And I simply do not see how this is done in a very few hours. So perhaps it just repeats an earlier order or something like that, but the time-frame to me is not realistic. That's all. But let's leave it at that now. Maybe it's not that important, after all.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I might be of assistance. Under 2D00313, we have an exhibit, a joint press release by Petar Zelenika and Arif Pasalic, and in this press release all those items are listed. So it's an agreement of the 21st of April, and that document is already an exhibit. And perhaps we can look it up in e-court and you can see, in the document, that it is an order that is also being sent to the 4th Corps of the BH Army for their information, to let them know that for their part, the HVO did what had been agreed the previous day. I only wanted to help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you, and I appreciate that. Let me put a different question. Was everything realised by 2.00 on that day? Was that complied with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Well, in an effort to achieve this agreement, Mr. Pellnas found me down there, and in an effort to achieve this solution, I strongly participated in this from the rear, from behind the scenes, so to speak. And it was signed by Mr. Zelenika and Mr. Pasalic, and one had to act very quickly. Tensions were running high, and I told you what happened with the group of the BH Army soldiers who had come to the Bulevar. And the situation got complicated again. After all this was complied with, but these are other problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, as far as the time element is concerned, I would like to provide you with my modest contribution. Now, I stand to be corrected. I'm looking at the B/C/S text, and I believe this is a telex. If you look at the font of the words, one has a feeling that this is a telex. And if you look at the left-hand side, it says "RBiH," an abridged version, "HZ HB, HVO, OZ GIH." So clearly time is of the essence. If you type this up, it takes five minutes for an expert secretary, at the very least, and then two seconds later it's transmitted via telex. We might have had an explanation had we had the original text. We might realised then that right at the top when you have a telex you have the time, the time it was sent, the day when it was received, and so on. So had we had the original, we would have seen this mentioned at the top of the page and perhaps on the other side, because this is a photocopy, we may have seen a stamp. The reason I'm saying this is because I've already come across such a case. Irrespective of this, and our colleague has mentioned this, all the people arrested should be freed by 2.00 on the 22nd of April. This is what I understand. All people arrested by the HVO and the ABiH must be exchanged by 1400 hours, on the basis of all-for-all. So if there are 100 on one side, 100 people should be exchanged. If the telex is sent in the morning, at 8.00 or 9.00, then you have enough time and ample time to execute the order. General Praljak, you have a better understanding of this type of document than we have. Can you tell us whether this text in B/C/S could be a telex sent by Mr. Lasic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By telex or packet communication. Just one more thing, Your Honour. At the time, there were no prisoners among the BH Army or the HVO because there had been no conflicts preceding this. Some people, a small number, was arrested by the military police of the HVO and the BiH Army during some minor skirmishes. There were a lot of reports about some shooting, there was some killings as well, and those people who, during the space of the two or three days, were brought in by the two police forces had to be exchanged, and it could have easily have been implemented within a short period of time. And a lot of this was indeed implemented within a short period of time. There was some positions taken in haste, there was no front-line. This had the initial appearance of a future possible conflict, but it was stopped and nipped in the bud.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have 20 minutes left. This was pointed out to me by the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, let me go back to a statement of yours with regard to this order. You said that when it comes to bullet point 11, if I understood you properly, the tasks contained in there had to be performed by the IPD Sector of the Defence Department, did I understand you properly, because it says here -- I apologise. Let's not overlap. Let me finish, and then you can take it from there. It says the assistant commander of the operational zone of the commander for the IPD is organising the meetings. Who was supposed to organise the meetings, the assistant commander or the Sector for the IPD of the Defence Department?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Nozica, I really do not know whether you do not want to understand, do not wish to understand, or is there something else?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, this is not my question. Tell me this: Does it say in the document the assistant commander -- and one more question. Is this at all something that was sent to the IPD Sector -- I apologise. The IPD Sector in the Defence Department, how should have the IPD Sector in the Defence Department supposed to know whether Mr. Lasic issued this order, if it was not even sent to their -- for their information? Just tell us "yes" or "no."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Nozica, I'm not going to answer your question because my answer should be what you want it to be. It is not necessary -- it was not necessary for Mr. Lasic to forward this to the IPD. The assistants would ask for the IPD to tell them what to talk about, what to discuss, what to discuss, what to relay to the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You've also told us, sir, that the chief of the SIS Administration appointed the assistants in the units, the assistants for SIS in the units. Did he appoint them or was he only proposing them?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He could have proposed their names. It could have been somebody else who proposed them, but he appointed them, and he put his signature on their appointment letters, and thus he became their chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, could you please look at documents, since we are talking about the appointments and whether he appointed them, and this is contrary to the decision on the internal organisation of the Defence Department. Let's look at the document P4756. I have just two documents to show you. I apologise. I really didn't -- wasn't able to prepare all the documents. I did not envisage the direction of my cross-examination, but both documents can be brought in the electronic courtroom because they have already been admitted into evidence. So I hope we will be able to bring them up in e-court. This is the transcript from the meeting of the Defence Department which was held on the 2nd of December, 1993. On the second page, if you can look at bullet point 1 of the transcript from this meeting - we've already seen it on several occasions - we can see that Mr. Matic represented the Main Staff at that meeting; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Under bullet point 2, it says that the book of rules and regulations governing the work and organisation of the Security and Information Service has been adopted, and it is also said here that Ivica Lucic provided a keynote address, and he also pointed out that he has encountered problems concerning the appointment of SIS officials at brigade levels because he had never been consulted about their appointment, and that in future this will no longer happen because the decision on the internal organisation of the Defence Department precisely regulates the appointment of such officials. He said this, Mr. Praljak, on the 2nd of September. If he had said something that was not correct, I'm sure that Mr. Matic would have intervened. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why Mr. Matic would have intervened, because Ivica Lucic did not do his part of the job, vis-a-vis the service, as the department allows him. He -- they were appointed, and he had to visit every one of them and make sure that he was the one who appointed them. If not, he would have -- he should have changed them or provided his consent. He says, I didn't do my job because somebody else did it, and then Matic should have intervened, according to you, but this is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Lucic did not do his job properly, somebody else did his part of the job, and now we're moving from de jure to the de facto. Let's look at document 2D944. This is also already an exhibit. This is a list of HVO units and SIS members, dated 19 November, and I am looking at this document just because of the date. The year is 1993. Can we turn to the last page, both in English and in Croatian, the last page, please? Mr. Lucic, in the month of November, in this report, which is submitted to Mr. Biskic, as we can see, he says here: "The majority of SIS personnel and units, their zones, brigades, battalions and MTDs, were appointed in violation of the valid decision on the internal organisation of the Defence Department dated 20 May 1993, which prescribed the procedure for appointing personnel to individual posts in -- and they don't have legal decisions to support their appointments. The proper procedure envisages that the assistant minister for security either appoints or proposes SIS personnel to be appointed to certain posts in the manning table. This procedure has mostly been violated so far in the way that brigade commanders appointed SIS personnel without seeking the approval of the assistant minister for security." Mr. Praljak, at the very beginning of my cross-examination we stated, as far as I remember, that the practice, when it came to appointment and many other things, was contrary to what was prescribed because of the times and the practice could not follow the procedure; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging by this document, it must be correct. I know that there are problems there. But look here, from the month of May until the month of November, he did not do his job. In the month of September, he said he would do it, he would follow the procedure, so he was -- what he was supposed to do was to tour the brigades and act in accordance with the regulations. This means that this man violated regulations and didn't do his job properly. And since he didn't do his job properly, what you are saying now is that the brigade commanders -- but, Ms. Nozica, this is not correct. People were supposed to do their job. If they didn't do it properly, it is inappropriate to say that the system was different, because they did not implement the system.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I didn't say anything -- I didn't say anything about the system. I just followed up on your remark that they were appointed by the assistant. Your remark was that the assistants for SIS in the units were appointed by the assistant for SIS or the chief for SIS of the head of the Defence Department. I showed you the documents that show what they show, and they show us that the practice was completely different. And just one more document that I would like to show you, which I owe you. I have not prepared it. It is P6137. This is an order on investigation about the events in Stupni Do. You told us that the order was also provided to Mr. Bandic, the order for investigation. I just want to -- you know this, you remember this order. It was, as we can see, provided to the OG commander, Ivica Rajic, as well as the commander of the Bobovac Brigade, Emil Harah. It arises from this order, as we can see, that this was not provided to the SIS Administration and especially not to Mr. Bandic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Milivoj Petkovic provides a very precise order about what the military part had to provide him with. I adhere by my words that the SIS has to do its job, irrespective of the order given to it by Milivoj Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm going to show two more documents referring to the IPD. I have sidetracked a little, but now I'm coming back to the IPD. Let's now look at the way the assistant commanders for IPD in the brigade report and who they report to. If we can look at document 2D653. You can also refer to e-court. I would like to see the top of the document, please, in the Croatian version. It says here the assistant brigade commander for IPD, Marin Zadric, who informs about an event which is not unimportant. It's an important event. He informs the Main Staff, the operations zone -- to operation zone the Rama Brigade and Mr. Dinko Zebic. Do you know where his position was in the month of April?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: He also informs Mr. Siljeg, and Veso Vegar as well. Mr. Praljak, can you remember whether the information in question from the IPD, the lower levels of the IPD, did it also arrive at the Main Staff? Can you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was their duty to inform -- I apologise. Ms. Nozica, they were duty-bound to inform units in the vicinity of the Main Staff what was going on. That was their duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And the last topic, Mr. Praljak -- I don't have much more time and I'm not going to be able to show you a lot of documents, but I believe that I have to still show a few. If we can bring up 3D1184, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This document was shown to you during direct examination. This is a weekly report. The following documents are directly referring to the work of the SIS. This is a weekly report which was submitted, as we can see from the stamp, to the SIS in Mostar, to the Defence Department there, and it was sent by Mr. Markesic, who at that point in time was employed at the SIS Centre Rama; is that correct, Mr. Praljak?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In addition to the SIS Centre, at the time there are also assistant commanders for SIS in the area in all of the units that existed and were deployed in the area?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so, but I can't tell you with any degree of certainty.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's look at the following document, the next one in your binder, which is 3831. I believe that Judge Antonetti has already shown you this document. These are all reports, the way they were sent and received, and who they were addressed to. Here, you see that in the original somebody added the words "Weekly Report." Mr. Luka Markesic is the signatory of this report. The date is 31 July, and at that time he was in the Rama Brigade. He was in charge of SIS there, and he reports about the events to the SIS of the OZ, the commander of the OZ, and the Rama Brigade commander; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So it would be true that this is the way the brigade's SIS service functioned?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But you see, Ms. Nozica, there are obviously procedures and how things should have been, and you see that at 1.00 after midnight, I was the one who held the meeting with the military police and in the previous document as well. Of course, he has to -- and if you saw this, he speaks about the security on the front-line. In other words, these things are all intertwined. It is not right that he informed his SIS about the security on the battle-field, whether I was behaving well and if I was good for the area, whether the situation had improved, the state of crime, whether the military police is functioning properly? Of course, that -- irrespective of the fact that he sent it to the SIS Administration that should have been specially engaged, he was duty-bound to send this to the brigade commander, because all of us, for crying out loud, we were all responsible if something didn't go well. You couldn't turn a blind eye and say, Okay, this is not functioning, but we will let things rest. Things should be different, but they're not. I've already spoken about the things that he's speaking about at the end, that the military police should be brought in. Yes, that's true, but where from? It is true that maybe one couldn't do more, but at least let's stick to the way things should have functioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, a very short question. Mr. Praljak, did you receive this report at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I did not, Your Honour. I knew about this because I was up there, so I, of course, knew about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You also knew about the group of 17 Muslim prisoners sent to Bugojno to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, nobody informed me about that, and this was a time when --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm speaking generally -- in general terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Something surprising, General Praljak. This report, which was sent to the SIS operations zone, very good, but if this report had been sent to the Department of Defence, a legal specialist at the Department of the Defence who reads this report, would he have realised that 17 Muslims had been sent to dig trenches, and then he could have warned the commander of the HVO to say, Look, there's a problem? Now, the fact that the report has stopped at the operations zone level, was that not a source of loss or lack of information in respect of the higher authority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. On the 31st of July, Mr. Luka Markesic was the assistant for SIS in the Rama Brigade, and, ex officio, he sent that to the SIS of the operations zone, and the SIS of the operations zone, in a report of theirs, will send it to the chief of SIS. As you were able to see in the previous document, when Mr. Markesic became the head of the SIS Centre for Rama, that is to say, when he was promoted to a higher post, he sent the report to the SIS Administration, the SIS Administration, that is to say, Ivo Lucic, who then probably had his lawyers and so on and then acted according to the information that they gained in conducting interviews and so on and so forth, because apart from the fact that he notes that 17 -- somebody took 17 people off, it was his duty now to investigate and see who the man was and name him, first and last name, or to ask the assistance of a higher service in the operations zone to send out more people to investigate. That's the crux of the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, if this document had been sent up to the upper echelons, they no doubt would have realised that there was a dual problem in paragraph 4, because it is mentioned that a woman was killed there during a mop-up operation. So that already raises the problem. That woman, was she a civilian, was she a combatant? It's a problem. If she was a civilian, why was she killed? So already that should have put people on alert. And then we see that there were houses that apparently were set on fire by unknown perpetrators. Now, that, too, raises a problem. If there is a military operation, how is it that during that military operation fire could be set to houses, unless the soldiers themselves did that? So someone in his office, I don't know where, reading this would say, Well, several problems are raised by this report. Now, if it stops at the operations zone level, where is the control? You say that the SIS and IPD, their main task was to exercise control over the action taken by the brigade commander. Now, if it stops at the operations zone's level, how is that control exerted? If we follow what you are saying, which is a logical standpoint, of course, well, this type of report should have gone directly to the Department of Defence so that, if needed, if Mr. Stojic was informed, the minister of defence would have called you and said, General Praljak, what's this operation about, what's going on? If things are working well at the level of Mr. Stojic, how can control actually take place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, I didn't actually say that, that it reached Mr. Stojic and that Mr. Stojic could control that. The SIS Centre in Rama was set up precisely in order to uncover, in a certain operation -- well, I saw that two houses were on fire. That's not contentious. But now we come to the problem, and the [indiscernible] of the matter, who and how set fire to those two houses? So I'm going to ask the commander, and he's going to say he used an inflammatory bullet because it was twilight, getting dark, So that I could see, and then I set fire to the roof. And that is militarily understandable. But how was this woman killed that you came across here? It was precisely the task of this man -- he's a very honest and decent man and did his job well, so the problem wasn't in intentions, but in that he just had one man, probably, and an old car, and that the number of problems were such that he wasn't able to uncover this, although there's a document which we don't have here where one or two killings were uncovered straight away and the perpetrators arrested. So, Your Honours, it wasn't a question of what they wished to do, their intentions, but what they could do, given the circumstances. It's easy to say, Well, Mr. Stojic should have done such and such, but what could he have done?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You say the question is not what we want, but what we can do. Unfortunately, in international humanitarian law, there are obligations, duties, that military officers are bound to. They are not responsible on the basis of what they can do, but under the obligations that arise from the relevant texts. That's the problem here. Anyway, Ms. Nozica has only three minutes left.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Judge Antonetti, Your Honour, on the basis of prescribed duties -- well, on the basis of prescribed duties and obligations, the American soldier -- because Mi Lai wasn't taken to task, but the people who did that, not the commander. So I state that 24 hours 'round the clock, I tried to do something. Now you're going to blame me and hold me guilty because I don't have wings, but I am assigned a task and then that is monitored to see how I carry out the task; orally, in writing, because I want to. Well, you're not going to take the mayor of Paris to task because there are ten killings every day, whereas the provisions say that killings are not permitted. I did my job very honestly and diligently, but because of the law of gravity, you can't stay up in the air if they throw you off a third -- the third floor of a building. I would fall, too. Markesic did his best, and we did catch dozens of people. They were put into prison and prosecuted. But, for heaven's sake, and I can't be held responsible for the catastrophe facing the world because I could not have uncovered it. Well, how should I have done that, if I issue honest orders or if I perhaps beat people up? Or hold on a minute --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have understood what you are telling us. You are telling us that you cannot control everything 24 hours a day. This is something you have said already and which you are saying again. It's on the record. I believe my colleague would like to ask you a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Indeed. Mr. Praljak, I may misunderstand the top part of this document, but it seems to me that it was also sent to the commander of the operations zone; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean P831?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it was sent to the SIS of the operations zone, the commander of the operations zone, and the commander of the Rama Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, today, earlier, we have again seen all those wonderful orders about how commanders must intervene to prevent crimes. This document rather clearly speaks of a war crime, taking prisoners to work on trenches. What did the zone operator do, the commander of the operations zone? Did he do his duty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'll repeat this for the hundredth time. On the 31st of July, Your Honours, at least 15.000 soldiers of the BH Army, from the 24th onwards, attacked me 'round the clock, 24 hours. You say there's no war, I don't have 20 dead a day, I don't have sabotage units infiltrated. Well, let's discuss it this way: I don't know what the zone's commander undertook, because we don't have a name as to who took the prisoners out for trench-digging. It was SIS's duty, so SIS is still searching. It made an observation, concluded something, and for the operations zone command or Rama Brigade command or Praljak to do something, this man has to say who did it, who committed the act, and launch an investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And in other cases, we have seen that commanders order such an investigation, but apparently not here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Trechsel, Your Honour, the SIS Centre ex officio would do this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, did it, did it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was their duty to. Well, yes, they were conducting an investigation, he says, I talked to these people, I investigated that, I asked about this. So when he's tabling this report, he knows about the fact, and he is duty-bound to continue his investigations further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry. There seems to be no trace of such an investigation, you just say so; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How do you know there is no trace? Because we don't have such a document, is that why? Now, at 1.00 a.m. I convened the military police. I shouted at them to get moving and take action about unrest of this kind and unruly behaviour of this kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I thought you did not know about these prisoners being taken to work in trenches. Did you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, no, I didn't know, Your Honour. I know about -- knew about the general quantity of disruptive behaviour, and the fighting we were engaged with, and the dozens of wounded that we had to see to, and everything else. All this looks quite different if you look at it in a laboratory with a -- in a test-tube, rather than knowing the situation as it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, irrespective of war crimes, this document also mentions something which, in military and technical terms, should have alerted the commander of the operations zone. It says that the middle of the text that there was an anti-tank mine that had been buried "on our territory," and a civilian had been killed and an 11-year-old child had been injured, as well as a soldier, which means, in military terms, that the "enemy," in inverted commas, had managed to place an anti-tank mine on your territory controlled by the HVO, and this had caused some damage. The operations zone's commander should have wondered how it was possible for the lines to be infiltrated for someone to pose such a mine. This could have been an issue, in military terms, unless one thinks that this mine had been there for a very long time. I don't know. This document is extremely well drafted and addresses all the issues. It should have been used by the commander. This is what the Judges would like to know, whether such a document is a document which is useful for the commander or not. This is a question one could put to an operations zone commander. Well, you might not be able to answer because you are not one of the addressees of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was there at that time, Your Honours, and our positions were hollow; that is to say, we didn't have enough soldiers. The operations commander was at the front-line, pursuant to my order, for many days with a rifle in his hands. And 1500 soldiers came in from Bugojno. They didn't look like human beings at all. And 15.000 refugees came from Bugojno, who didn't look like humans at all, in a small town which just has 3.000 inhabitants normally. And so our lines were hollow. I would take a step forward and two steps back, or one step forward, one step back, and this went on day and night. You have to put up 15.000 people, take them towards Croatia. 1.500 soldiers were distraught, not all of them, but a large number had lost their nearest. So this was a situation that the French Ministry of Defence would have to deal with, with all the resources it has at its disposal, that kind of institution of that size and capacity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, I told you that you had three minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will do my best.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, you said that the SIS in the operational zone, the major addressee was supposed to inform the SIS Administration in Mostar; is that so?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the logic dictates that that would be the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And the commander of the operational zone, whom did he have to inform, according to the logic of the matter?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: About what?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, we were talking about the document, and you said, speaking about this document, that the operational zone SIS was supposed to inform the SIS Administration?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. But here we see, when it comes to the actions that are to be taken when the obligation is in place, whose obligation. You said that this was a document from the SIS Centre. Well, this is not a document from the SIS Centre.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: That's what I understood.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters' note: The speakers are kindly asked not to overlap, because we will stop interpreting.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: On the 31st of July, 1993, Mr. Luka Markesic was the chief in the Rama Brigade SIS, and Mr. Praljak, I will conclude by saying that this document was sent to the Rama Brigade commander. That's not controversial. Can we look in the e-court. Just once again, you said it was the obligation of the SIS Centre to undertake an investigation, but let us look again - that's my last document and my last question - whose obligation it was under Article 27 of the Decree on District Military Courts. It's the document P00592. I will read it. You don't have to read it. Your Honour Judge Antonetti, I said it just for the transcript, it says: "The commander of a military unit and of a military establishment is duty-bound to take all measures to prevent the perpetrator of a crime being prosecuted ex officio, not to be able to conceal himself or abscond, to preserve all the evidence of a crime," and so on and so forth. So you have already been shown this, and you answered when Judge Antonetti asked you about this. And in light of the fact that the commander of the brigade was informed about all those events, was he then duty-bound to ensure that the investigative actions are taken, as is indicated here?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He could have done it, but he was not duty-bound. It says here a perpetrator of a crime, if a commander observed or caught them. Well, you can see what it says here, that he doesn't hide or abscond. The brigade commander cannot even catch him, because the act -- the crime happened three or five days ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Just one follow-up question, and then I'll complete my examination. And is it not that the brigade commander was supposed to order, and perhaps he may have done so - we don't know that - to his assistant, Find this person, interrogate that person? Was that the duty?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What person?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, the person who committed something in his area of responsibility, something that constitutes a crime.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This was the duty of the assistant for SIS to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: It is high time that you would accept, first of all, that the three minutes are over, number 1. Number 2, the -- actually, what we have heard from the interpreters, that they will stop interpreting if you continue this overlapping, and I am fully with them. So please kindly obey the orders. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, Judge Prandler has just said that your three minutes were over. You need to finish. If you have one last question, put it straight away, and then we shall have the break, since we need to keep an eye on the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I accept fully what Judge Prandler said. This completes my cross-examination, but I would like to apologise. It's impossible, Your Honour Judge Prandler -- well, I apologise to all the interpreters. Sometimes it is impossible to control over every word and to say it as slowly as one should because, after all, this is a job that sometimes gets us carried away, even us lawyers, who should really be aware of it, and let alone the witnesses. It's impossible to do it. I'm trying to, and I obviously am not succeeding, so I apologise once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Nozica. I would also like to say that I am at fault sometimes because I speak too fast, and I'm also responsible for this. We're going to have a break now. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Just one quick item, Mr. President. I could offer perhaps a clarification. There was some testimony earlier about Exhibit P02030, 2030. It was the document that Judge Mindua had asked about, and then Judge Trechsel had a number of questions about the time-frame, execution of Miljenko Lasic's order. Ms. Pinter directed the Trial Chamber to a press release. I thought I would -- I could also direct the Trial Chamber to P02054. The general made a reference to General Pellnas who was involved at the time in those events, and 2054 is General Pellnas's report about that time-frame, the 19th, 20th, to the 22nd of April, and it provides additional background about the events that led up to the document that Judge Trechsel and Judge Mindua asked about. So thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your clarification. We shall scrutinize Exhibit P02054, which is General Pellnas's report. We shall have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, you wanted to say something?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Your Honours. I tried to complete my examination in the time that was allotted to me, and at the same time the objections to my speed were quite justified, and I failed to thank Mr. Praljak for his answers. And I'm sorry for failing to do so before.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. A very good afternoon to you and to everyone in the courtroom. Since I do not have as much time as I expected, I prepared my cross-examination last week, but I will have to reorganise it now because of the circumstance, and I will have to skip documents that are in your binders. We will deal with binder number 1, the first topic, borders of the former Yugoslavia. And if I have enough time, I will go back to some of the documents in this set at the end of my cross-examination. Now I would like to skip this and go to the next topic behind the second blue tab, and that's the conflict between the BH Army and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Ms. Alaburic. I'm sorry, you're telling us that you didn't have time. You have been granted 45 minutes. If you feel you need some extra time, we will take it off your time credit, because you have been granted a certain number of hours. It's for you to decide. If you would like to have an extra hour, this will be taken off the extra time which has been grant -- or the time granted to you to hear all your witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you very much for this offer. And if you allow me, I would like to postpone my final decision on this until the end of my cross-examination, because unfortunately you now brought me into a situation where I have to choose between the testimony of my own client and General Praljak, so I have to think about the repercussions of both options. So let us now move to the second set of the documents. The topic is the duration of the conflict between the BH Army and the HVO. It seems to me that this quite important and should serve well by way of introduction.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the first document that you have, document 2D1183, 2D1183. That's the Law on Special Rights enjoyed by persons who receive military rewards and citations. Please go ahead, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Alaburic, I would be most grateful if you could say which binder it is. I seem to have found it now. It's in binder 1, the first one in orange colour. Is that where we are?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, it's in binder number 1, but it's not the first topic. The first topic is borders of the former Yugoslavia, the republics from the former Yugoslavia. But it is the second topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General Praljak, I'm only interested in Article 1 of this law, where it says that the defence -- the war of defence and liberation in Bosnia and Herzegovina lasted from the 18th of September, 1991, until the 23rd of December, 1995. General Praljak, could you tell us, if you know, what happened in September 1991, on the 18th of September?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the attack on the village of Ravno.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And do you know what happened on the 23rd of December, 1995, which is the last day of the war?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the signing of the Dayton Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. So if we now calculate how long the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina lasted, in accordance with the legislation, that would be four years three months, or a total of fifty-one months. I think I calculated this correctly.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us look at what was going on in 1991 between Croats and Muslims. In 1991, were Croats and Muslims in any kind of a war conflict?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In 1992, if we disregard the sporadic incidents, in particular the one in Prozor in October 1992, can we then say that, as a rule, in 1992 there were no conflicts, armed conflicts, between Croats and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. A question of mathematics. My calculations make 41 and a half months.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Trechsel, well, I rounded off the figures. That's why I said "51." But if you say it's 51 and a half, well, that's not the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: No, 48 and a half.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Four years, that's 48 months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I've got the wrong date. I deeply apologise. My time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's move on to the year of 1993. If we disregard the events in Gornji Vakuf and in Central Bosnia in January, can we agree that the open conflict between the BH Army and the HVO did not exist up until sometime in mid-April 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we can agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can we also agree, General, that from mid-April 1993 until the 30th of June, 1993, that there were conflicts, but at the same time there were intense negotiations to achieve a cease-fire and a peaceful solution for the conflicts?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we can agree on that. Those efforts on our part continued even later on, but were in vain.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If I understand your evidence correctly, on the 30th of June, 1993 -- well, you mark that day as a watershed of sorts, and you say that a total, all-out war began on that day; did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After that, there was no going back until the military situation was resolved, until it could be seen whether the BH Army would achieve its goals or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In this courtroom, other persons said the same, and I will just list Witness BC, who at page 18337 of the transcript, said that this event in late June fundamentally changed the situation. Would you agree with this assessment by Witness BC?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. One could say that in Central Bosnia, it was a little bit earlier, from their point of view, but generally speaking that was the day after which, unfortunately, the war escalated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So we're in the year 1994. Can we agree that the conflict went on up until the end of March 1994, more or less, and that the Washington Agreement was signed then?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: That would mean, General Praljak, that from approximately 1st of April, 1994, the BH Army and the HVO, and the civilian authorities, were working together and were working intensively on finding ways to work together; is that so?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And in 1995, which is defined here as a war year, the cooperation between Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO was completely unobstructed, they fought the same enemy; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm sure that Judge Trechsel will correct me if I'm wrong, but according to my calculation the conflict between Croats and Muslims lasted approximately for 12 months, from mid-April 1993 until the end of March 1994. Would that be the case, General?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and the all-out war actually lasted even less.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, if we take only this period and correlated it to the whole of the war period, we will see that the conflict between Croats and Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina existed in the course of the 23 per cent of the overall war, which would mean that in 77 per cent of the wartime period, Croats and Muslims were allies, fighting a common enemy. General, your mathematical mind has probably come up with the figures already, and could you agree with my calculations about the time when cooperation existed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your calculation is good. But, Ms. Nozica [as interpreted], you also have to say that the conflict between Croats and Muslims did not take place in the entire territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. There were a number of areas where the HVO and BiH Army were not in conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that. I know, General Praljak, that my learned friend Ms. Nozica made quite an impression on you, but let me remind you that my name is Ms. Alaburic. I know you know that and you misspoke when you called me "Ms. Nozica." Okay, well, let's look at the next document. I would like us now to analyse the cooperation with the Croatian Army. Let us look at 4D1297, 4D1297. These are conclusions reached at a meeting in Jablanica attended by the HVO and BiH Army on the 29 [as interpreted] February 1995. The representatives were Tihomir Blaskic and Rasim Delic. General, the year 1995 was the year when the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina was already in place; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at bullet point 3 in these conclusions. I would like to correct the date on the record. The conclusions were reached on the 22nd of February, not 29 February, as has been recorded. Let's look at bullet point 3. It says: "Measures shall be taken to initiate a meeting between the chief of the Main Staff of the HV, Army General Janko Bobetko, the chief of the Main Staff of the HVO, Major General Tihomir Blaskic, and the commander of the General Staff of the BH Army, General Rasim Delic, to agree on joint tasks in the struggle against the Serbian-Montenegrin aggressor, and this will be within the context of terminating UNPROFOR's mandate." General, am I to conclude from this that in February 1995, the representatives of the HVO and the BiH Army wanted military cooperation with the HV, with the Croatian Army, in the struggle against the Serbian and Montenegrin aggressor? Was that indeed the case?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the case. This resulted in an operation that prevented Bihac from experiencing the destiny of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can we now look at bullet point 10, where it says: "To continue the joint struggle against the Serb and Montenegrin aggressor, the joint command will have the role --" I'm interested in this joint staff. Was that joint staff ever established?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the following document, which is 4D1454. This is a memo coming from the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, covering the conversation that took place in Sarajevo on the 14th of June, 1994, or, rather, the talks held in Sarajevo on 14 June 1994. General, you were present at that meeting. Do you remember the meeting?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: At the end of the document, could you look at bullet point 3, where it says: "The concept of the defence of the Confederation." And it says: "It has been agreed to form a joint team which will start working as soon as possible. "General Anton Tus will head the team on behalf of the Republic of Croatia."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: That's how it was?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So according to this document, General Praljak, in June 1994 there were already talks about the establishment of a joint staff, a joint team, and a joint operation involving the BiH Army and the Croatian Army; was that the case?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was with the blessing and after a lot of persuasion by the American side.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General Praljak, during your testimony so far, you have told us that the then president of the Republic of Croatia, Dr. Franjo Tudjman, proposed a military agreement to Alija Izetbegovic at the outset of the conflict in 1992. Was that the case?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He even proposed that much earlier, as we could see in Filipovic's book. Even earlier than that, Bosnia-Herzegovina was urged to adopt cooperation between Slovenia, the Republic of Croatia, and Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, this was to no avail.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If I recorded your words properly, you told us that Alija Izetbegovic had not accepted that proposal because he did not want to antagonise the Serbs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct. This was the card that he still wished to play, a possible agreement with the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, in 1994 and 1995, if there had been a military cooperation between the two armies of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Croatian Army, or, rather, would you say that that cooperation which existed was successful, and is it true that the Americans stopped the Croatian Army at the very entrance into Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. If there hadn't been the agreement in place and the green light was not given by the Americans, Bihac would have fallen and the Croatian Army, which was cooperating with the HVO and the Bosnia and Herzegovina Army, would not have succeeded. As things stand, it did succeed to suppress the Army of Republika Srpska and did reach Banja Luka, and it was fully prepared to record a full military success. However, there was a telephone call to President Tudjman to stop the army. The Dayton Accord was signed, and the Serbs were given 49 per cent of the territory, which is absolutely inconceivable.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, I have a question for you now which for some other witness might be a call for speculation. However, given your knowledge of the situation on the ground, I believe that your answer will not be speculation, but rather an assessment that will be given some weight in those proceedings. My question to you is this: If, in 1992, Alija Izetbegovic had accepted the invitation for military cooperation with the Republic of Croatia, would the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina against the Army of Republika Srpska have been different than it was in the 51 months?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... General. Just for the record, Mr. President, we do object to the question. It does call for speculation, and it's really not testimony that's useful. Reams have been -- could be written about what could have happened, what might have happened, if this or that had happened, and so this sort of speculation is not helpful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I expected this kind of objection. That's why my question was preceded with the introduction. I still believe that this is not speculation and that General Praljak has demonstrated his analytical capabilities and inclinations, and that he also showed us that he is very knowledgeable and well informed about the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: One more question about this. If the military cooperation with the Republic of Croatia had started in 1992, is it absolutely certain that there would never have been a war between the Croats and the Muslims? What do you think about that, General Praljak?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that the first question was a call for speculation. If, in 1992, we managed to liberate Stolac and Mostar and stop them at Livno with the newly-created HVO, if we had been together with the BH Army and the Croatian Army, and in Bosnia-Herzegovina you're talking about at least 250.000 to 270.000 armed men, I'm absolutely certain when I say that the Army of Republika Srpska would not have been able to prevail.
